The Right To Be Left Alone

There is no right to be left alone. This would cancel out the right to free speech, which is what we need to fight for.

As for leaving society, we can't do that, either. Men have been hiding their heads in the sand for decades. It doesn't work.

I completely agree, but there is also no right that one individual's speech can be foisted onto another. I think that's more the point of the article. The author is not calling for silence, or even silence in a particular venue. He is pontificating on the right of one individual to not listen or agree with another's (perhaps more PC) speech. To have the option of not listening to that speech. I didn't see anywhere in the post where the author was calling for silence. He was calling for the ability to walk away.

As for leaving society, I would not say that is not working. Germany now has the fastest aging population in the world, due to low birth rates (Germany has a very strong women's rights lobby). Marriage rates in the US are at an all time low, and youngans looking to marry are also at an all time low. Those in their 20's and 30's have assessed marriage as a business proposition, and men found it non-beneficial, and they are walking away from the table. Women have decided that the most effective way to get men back to the marriage table is to harass men in media and in political narrative. That may have worked for a little while, but it's effectiveness is waning. Hence all the "where have the good men gone?" articles. Those men are still here. Women just moved the goal post one time to many and the fuckers didn't come back out after halftime.

The author points to areas such as online gaming where, according to the author, younger men have been using as an escape from the political correctness they can be accosted with. Recent events, i.e. GamerGate, have made online gaming about politics. The author is lamenting that there isn't a facet of society besides sitting in your house with the lights off, no TV/radio/internet, that one can find peace from the constant agenda pushing that anyone with a mic and a camera is guilty of.

I agree that everyone should have the right to be left alone if they so choose. That doesn't mean that it should be expected that others are silenced in a public place, but that people should be able to create or have places they can go and politics are checked at the door, metaphorically speaking.

As an example, if I run a forum I should have every right to dictate what I want to be allowed so long as it is legal to share it. I have the same expectations for my physical home, I should have the say about what I want to hear or talk about in my home. Out in public, people can say what they want but I do not have to listen. That's the point, I believe. Others can speak all they want, but those that don't want to hear it should have a place to be left alone.
Is that really a desirable outcome? Wouldn't it be nicer to just fix what's broken with society instead of forcing people to withdraw into their own little world?

I finished Texhnolyze a couple of days ago and wrote up a spoiler-y discussion, if anyone would like to participate. If you haven't seen the show, then you're in the right place, because I'm about to pitch it to you, spoiler-free.

The surface-level synopsis of this show suggests a dystopian, underground future, where lost limbs can be artificially replaced through a hybridization of man and machine, called texhnolyzation. The story mostly follows Ichise, a purposeless man, as he is sucked into the conflicts of the subterranean city of Lux.

Texhnolye is a great example of the old writer's adage, "Show; don't tell." Anyone who's at all familiar with anime as a medium is probably well-acquainted with the monotonous monologues and extensive exposition that usually constitute world-building (looking at you, first episode of Fate/Zero). Even outside of anime the authors of fictional worlds and stories often feel that the best way to clue you in to the state of their make-believe land is to tell you straight-out; whether that be by just telling you or making a character do it.

Texhnolyze, on the other hand, tells you virtually nothing through monologue or dialogue. The viewer is left to glean the setting through the characters and their interactions with the world. The reason that most works simply tell you where you are and what is happening is because it is incredibly difficult to so eloquently present your setting in a way that the consumer can infer everything you intend. Texhnolyze does this superbly, imparting a definite tone and feeding the viewer information about the world through nonconventional means. If you've been paying attention, then you know most of what's happened before you get to the episode where they explain parts of the story (an episode which is notably very near the end of the series, if not the last episode).

Showing, and not telling, is not the only arena in which Texhnolyze can be championed. Texhnolyze deftly explores many themes, and these themes are interpreted by different people differently. I found that Texhnolyze had a lot to say about society, evolution, and survival, and the volatile relation between the three. From what I hear, however, people draw different conclusions as to the ultimate theme of the show. It is a beautiful thing to create a portrait from which people can each take something unique away as per their life experiences. To not let one's own voice drown out the ideas of the consumer takes skill, and such feats are executed in Texhnolyze.

In conclusion, Texhnolyze can be aptly described as sublime. It is a very subdued show with a slow pace that allows you to absorb everything it has to offer. Its economic use of dialogue and subtle use of imagery make it a truly enthralling piece from start to finish. If you like more artistic titles, or really enjoy thematically deep dystopian sci-fi, then Texhnolyze is right up your alley.
